title: Akron Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Akron well records show a 120-foot median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical finished-well costs of $10,200-$18,600.
h1: What Akron, Colorado Well Records Mean for Buyers
intro_html:
Buying land near Akron means looking beyond the presence of a well. The local record shows 405 permitted wells, with 241 recorded as constructed. Of those, 270 report total depth, 74 report pump yield, and 26 report static water level.

That is enough to establish useful local expectations, but not enough to guarantee a result on a particular parcel. Neighboring wells, the aquifer named on the permit, access for a rig, and the intended household use all matter. This area includes plains sediment and alluvium, along with permits naming fractured bedrock, the Ogallala, and Chadron aquifers.

sections.heading: Akron well depths range from shallow plains wells to 800 feet
sections.html:
The median Akron well is 120 feet deep, and the middle half runs from 98 to 200 feet. The depth distribution is fairly concentrated: 25% are under 100 feet, while 63% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 11% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 1% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well is 800 feet.

For a drilling bid, use the 120-foot median as a planning point rather than a promise. A quote based on a 100-foot hole can change substantially if the driller must continue toward the local 200-foot range or beyond. Check wells nearest the lot, especially in the same aquifer and geologic setting.

sections.heading: Most Akron wells report useful production, but yield still varies
sections.html:
Among the 74 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.5 and 20.0 gallons per minute. The records show 70% producing more than 15 gallons per minute, 26% between 5 and 15, and 4% between 1 and 5. None of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a stronger production picture than many buyers expect from an individual rural well, but it is not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. A yield test measures that well, not the entire property. Confirm the permit's allowed use, test the pump and pressure system, and ask for a written production record before relying on the supply.

sections.heading: Akron water levels do not show a simple dropping trend
sections.html:
The recorded static water level has a median depth of 83 feet, with the middle half between 63 and 96 feet below the surface. In decade groupings, the median measured depth was 88 feet in the 2010s and 64 feet in the 2020s.

That change points to a shallower measured water level in the newer group, not a declining water table. The result should be treated cautiously because only 26 records report static water level, and measurements can reflect different locations, seasons, well construction, and pumping conditions. A buyer should obtain a current measurement and compare it with nearby wells rather than infer a basin-wide trend from the decade figures.

sections.heading: Akron has a long permit history and several recurring drillers
sections.html:
Well permitting around Akron reaches back to the 1950s, when 26 permits were issued. The record shows 15 in the 1960s, 30 in the 1970s, 42 in the 1980s, 58 in the 1990s, 55 in the 2000s, 55 in the 2010s, and 20 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc (Twiss, Raymond L.) with 25 wells, Stewart Drilling Co. (Stewart, Dennis W.) with 23, and Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.) with 23. Those counts describe permit history, not current availability or a recommendation. Verify licensing, scope, casing and grout details, testing, and scheduling directly.

sections.heading: A median-depth Akron well can cost $10,200 to $18,600 finished
sections.html:
For Akron's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $4,200 to $6,600. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $10,200 to $18,600.

Those figures are a budgeting range, not a fixed bid. The final number can move with depth, access, casing and grout requirements, power distance, trench length, pump size, and site conditions. Ask for separate line items for drilling, completion, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, and testing so a low per-foot quote does not hide the rest of the installation.

sections.heading: PFAS, septic layout, and permit limits deserve a close review
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. There are no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped facts, but that does not make every well automatically safe. Test existing water for the conditions relevant to the property, and review nearby environmental records before closing.

Low yield and dry holes remain site-specific risks even where the reported median yield is 15.0 gallons per minute. A new well also needs proper casing and grout, separation from septic components, and enough room for construction and maintenance. Have the county and Colorado DWR confirm the permit, allowable household use, and any augmentation requirement before designing the home.

sections.heading: Before buying or building near Akron, verify the exact lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit number, construction record, well location, depth, aquifer, pump information, and water-quality history. Compare the property with nearby records in Akron and, when useful, surrounding areas such as Otis, Hillrose, Snyder, Brush, Merino, and Yuma. The closest comparable wells are more useful than a countywide average.

For vacant land, confirm that the proposed well location, septic system, driveway, house, and electrical route fit together before excavation. For an existing home, run the pump, measure static and pumping levels, inspect the pressure tank, and obtain a current water test. A permit is not the same as a guaranteed water supply, and household-use rights depend on the permit and applicable state rules.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Akron, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Akron is 120 feet. The middle half runs from 98 to 200 feet, while 63% are between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest record is 800 feet. For a property-specific estimate, compare nearby wells with the same aquifer and geology instead of relying on the median alone.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Akron, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $4,200 to $6,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,200 to $18,600. Access, final depth, equipment, and site layout can move the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Akron wells produce?
faq.a: Among Akron records reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.5 to 20.0. The records show 70% above 15 gallons per minute, 26% between 5 and 15, and 4% between 1 and 5. That describes recorded wells, not a guarantee for a new hole.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Akron?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. There are 9 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so a buyer should obtain a current laboratory water test and review nearby records. Existing homes should be tested before closing, and new wells should be tested after construction and disinfection.

faq.q: Are Akron well water levels going down?
faq.a: The median recorded static water level was 88 feet below surface in the 2010s and 64 feet in the 2020s. That indicates a shallower measured level in the newer group, not a simple decline. Only 26 records report static water level, and conditions vary by well, season, and measurement method, so confirm the specific property.
